problem: Many teams research and wire up the same open-source AI parts on their own, and their private versions drift apart.
who_has_it: Teams building AI systems from open-source parts.
why_it_matters: Time goes to plumbing and re-research instead of the product, and the result is unproven.
why_hard: Parts change often and the best one depends on the case, so a choice made once goes out of date unless it is measured again.
existing_attempts: Curated lists of hubs, one-off private integrations, and picking by taste.

problem: Lists of hubs say what exists, not which works best for a given job or how well parts work together. Public benchmarks rank some parts, but rarely on the cases a team actually has, and rarely together.
who_has_it: Teams building AI systems from open-source parts.
why_it_matters: Teams pick by reputation or by one public score, so the part they use may not be the best for their job, and they cannot show that it is.
why_hard: The parts change weekly and "best" depends on the case, so only repeated measurement keeps a choice honest.
existing_attempts: Curated lists of hubs, public benchmarks and leaderboards, scores vendors report about their own products, and picking by taste.
auto_status: open: unmeasured the-world, the-subconscious, the-mind, connected-system-operations

problem: When a system is wired to one hub, that hub's outage, price change or shutdown can stop the system or raise its cost, and switching usually means changing code.
who_has_it: Teams building AI systems from open-source parts.
why_it_matters: Users lose service, or the team pays more, until someone rewrites the connection.
why_hard: Hubs expose different interfaces, so a second hub is rarely ready to take over without new code.
existing_attempts: Retries, a second provider wired by hand, and routers that fail over between model vendors.

problem: Each part is usually tuned and chosen on its own, so a part can be kept for how well it does alone even when the whole gains little from it or pays more for it.
who_has_it: Teams building AI systems from open-source parts.
why_it_matters: The assembled system can carry parts that add cost or delay without making it better, and the team cannot easily tell which ones.
why_hard: A part's value depends on the other parts and on real tasks, so judging it means running the whole with and without it, which takes time and real cases.
existing_attempts: End-to-end tests and demos of the whole, and benchmarks of each part alone. People assembling open-source parts have no shared, measured way to judge what each part adds to a whole.

problem: AI systems are usually built around one product's data, so another system cannot give the hub its own APIs, databases and files without rewriting parts.
who_has_it: Teams that want to apply the hub to a system of their own.
why_it_matters: Without a way to plug in another system's data, the hub stays useful mainly to the product it was built beside.
why_hard: Each system keeps its context in different places and in different shapes.
existing_attempts: Hand-written adapters inside each product.

problem: A request is often answered from whatever context is at hand (the recent chat, a fixed set of files), so the AI sees too much to use well or too little to answer.
who_has_it: People who rely on an AI to answer one request well.
why_it_matters: An answer built on the wrong information is usually wrong, however well the model reasons.
why_hard: What bears on a request is only known after the request is read, and each source has its own cost.
existing_attempts: Fixed prompts and retrieval tuned by taste.

problem: Most AI assistants use the same rule for every person, so they ask a person who wanted them to go ahead and act without asking a person who wanted to be asked.
who_has_it: People who delegate work to AI representatives.
why_it_matters: People stop delegating when the AI interrupts for nothing or surprises them.
why_hard: Each person wants a different balance, and the balance changes as trust grows.
existing_attempts: One fixed rule for asking, set by the product.

problem: A part that was best a few months ago can be overtaken by a newer one, and without a fresh comparison the team using it often does not notice.
who_has_it: Teams building AI systems from open-source parts.
why_it_matters: Time goes to plumbing and re-research instead of the product, and the result is unproven.
why_hard: The parts change weekly and "best" depends on the case, so only repeated measurement keeps a choice honest.
existing_attempts: Curated lists of hubs, one-off private integrations, and picking by taste.

problem: A system's own knowledge, in its internal APIs, databases and local files, cannot be offered to the AI without code written for that system.
who_has_it: Teams that apply the hub to a system of their own.
why_it_matters: The AI then answers from the web and its model, and misses what the system itself knows.
why_hard: Each system keeps its knowledge in different places, formats and permissions.
existing_attempts: Hand-written adapters inside each product.

problem: Most AI assistants decide when to ask by one fixed rule, so one person is interrupted for steps they would have allowed and another is surprised by steps they would have wanted to approve.
who_has_it: People who delegate work to AI representatives.
why_it_matters: Each wrong interruption or wrong surprise lowers the person's trust.
why_hard: A risk signal says how risky a step is, not whether this person would want to be asked.
existing_attempts: A fixed list of steps that need approval.

problem: In many assistants a correction changes the next reply but is not kept, so the person has to give it again.
who_has_it: People who work with an AI representative.
why_it_matters: Repeating a correction costs the person the time the AI was meant to save.
why_hard: Feedback is given in many forms and concerns different behaviours, so it must be tied to what it corrected.
existing_attempts: Pinned instructions, long prompts, and memory features that save notes without checking that a correction is followed later.

problem: People make requests where they already work (a chat, a task list, the action items of a meeting), and a system that only answers one input cannot take them in, so requests are lost, answered twice or answered to the wrong person.
who_has_it: Anyone who runs an AI for a team.
why_it_matters: A request that does not arrive is not answered, and a person who is not recognized can be served with someone else's authority.
why_hard: Every system has different places requests come from, and each arrives in its own shape.
existing_attempts: A chat bot per channel, task-queue integrations, and meeting assistants that list action items without acting on them.

problem: While the AI works the person cannot see what it reads, changes and runs or which helper is acting, cannot stop it without losing the work, resume it, send a correction and see it taken up, or approve a risky step before it happens, and each surface and harness does this differently.
who_has_it: People who delegate deep work to an AI and watch it from a terminal, a chat page or a task page.
why_it_matters: A person who cannot see, stop or steer the work either watches nothing and trusts blindly or does not delegate; a surprise that cannot be undone costs more than the work saved.
why_hard: Harnesses report progress in different shapes (strings, stream lines, trees), stopping and steering reach them differently, and a screen written for one harness breaks for the next.
existing_attempts: Each terminal agent has its own screen (Claude Code, Codex CLI, opencode, Aider and others); a consumer's terminal, chat and task modal each re-implement part of it.

problem: An AI representative that works for several people across many projects keeps no history of its own (what it was asked, what it produced, which sources it used, how it was corrected), so each request meets a stranger; and what it does keep can reach an asker who may not see the project it came from.
who_has_it: Teams whose representatives work across projects and people, and characters with no person behind them.
why_it_matters: Without its own history a representative cannot stay consistent or improve, which is the reason to have one; a leak across projects breaks trust.
why_hard: Its history is written by different people in different projects, so keeping it per representative and showing it only to askers who may see its source pull in opposite directions.
existing_attempts: Persona prompts, per-persona profile notes and chat history windows, none fenced by project access.

problem: A guard or reviewer added around a model or harness is often kept because it seems careful, without evidence that it catches anything the model or harness would miss alone.
who_has_it: Teams that add safety and review layers to an AI that acts.
why_it_matters: Each layer costs money and time and can block ordinary work, so a guard that adds nothing makes the system worse.
why_hard: The native checks of a model or harness change with every release, so a guard's gain has to be measured again on the same cases, with and without it.
existing_attempts: Layers added by judgment and kept by habit.

problem: AI answers often claim more than the evidence behind them supports, and the reader cannot tell which claim is unsupported.
who_has_it: People who rely on an AI answer.
why_it_matters: A claim without support looks the same as a claim with it.
why_hard: Support has to be checked claim by claim against sources the reader can open.
existing_attempts: Asking the model to cite, without checking the citation.

problem: What the planning and responding AI sees for a request is whatever was wired to it: earlier requests and goals are missing, the right information is not found, or too much of it is pasted in.
who_has_it: The person whose request is answered, and the team that has to debug an answer that missed something it should have known.
why_it_matters: An answer is only as good as the view it was written from, and a view that is too thin or too full costs quality and money on every request.
why_hard: The long view, the finding and the planning have different measures and change for different reasons, so improving one by hand hides whether another got worse.
existing_attempts: Long prompts that carry everything, a vector store with one retrieval setting, and memory features tied to one product.

problem: Parts assembled together drift: one does another part's work, hides its own failure or claims more than its evidence shows, and no part is responsible for the coherence of the whole.
who_has_it: Teams that assemble an AI from many parts.
why_it_matters: A whole that passes every part's test can still contradict itself in use.
why_hard: A part cannot see the whole, and the whole is judged from the user's seat, not part by part.
existing_attempts: Per-part tests and hand review of the whole.

problem: One public benchmark is trusted alone to rank parts, although it may measure a different task, be saturated or leaked into training data, and its source is rarely checked.
who_has_it: Anyone choosing AI parts from published scores.
why_it_matters: A pick that rests on one score can be wrong for the job and still look certain.
why_hard: Public numbers differ in task, date and method, and a stage built from one source cannot tell which differences matter.
existing_attempts: Leaderboards quoted whole, and figures a vendor reports about its own product.

problem: A part is ranked best overall, but which part is best depends on the circumstance (a cost limit, a speed limit, a language, the size of the input), so the single winner can be wrong for many users.
who_has_it: Teams that use the hub's default with a budget or latency limit that differs from the measured one.
why_it_matters: The default is right on average and wrong for a case that is common for the user.
why_hard: Every circumstance multiplies the cases to run, and a variant of a part is easy to leave out of the comparison.
existing_attempts: One overall leaderboard per task, with the settings left to each user.

problem: An agent harness used on a flat subscription is slow and spends more tokens than the work needs, partly because the context it is given is poor and partly because it repeats work through sub-agents and recursion.
who_has_it: Teams that run agents on a Claude Code or similar subscription.
why_it_matters: Cost shows up as time and as the usage limit, so a dear harness stops other work.
why_hard: Cost depends on the harness, the context handed to it, its use of sub-agents and the model together, so changing one at a time hides the effect of the others.
existing_attempts: Picking a harness by reputation, and trimming prompts by hand.

problem: A factual or research answer often cites a web page, or nothing, instead of the papers and data that bear on it, so the reader cannot check it.
who_has_it: Anyone who asks an AI a factual or research question.
why_it_matters: A claim that cannot be checked cannot be trusted.
why_hard: Papers and data sit behind many different search interfaces, and relevance is judged case by case.
existing_attempts: Web search alone.

problem: Each part that needs a model or a tool is wired to one vendor or one integration directly, so a better model or tool outside the system cannot be adopted without rewriting parts.
who_has_it: Anyone building on the hub, and every part that asks a model or uses a tool.
why_it_matters: Models, prices and tools change outside the system faster than any part is rewritten, so hand wiring turns each improvement into a project.
why_hard: The measure that decides a good model or tool is external and changes with the outside, so no fixed wiring stays right.
existing_attempts: One vendor SDK called from every part, and per-product tool lists.

problem: Many products rebuild each app connection (calendar, drive, notes, chat) with their own screen, storage and tool code, so a new app costs code in every layer and often arrives months after hubs list it.
who_has_it: Teams whose users want their own apps connected to an AI.
why_it_matters: Users get the apps a team had time to wire, not the apps they use, and each connection is a new place for credentials to leak.
why_hard: Each app has its own sign-in, scopes and tools, and a user's credentials must never reach another user's turns.
existing_attempts: Hand-written adapters per app; integration hubs that expose many apps as MCP tools but leave the connect screen, credential storage and consent to each product.

problem: An app connection (a calendar, a drive, a chat) is often served better by several hubs combined than by any one, but a product usually wires a single hub and hand-writes the rest.
who_has_it: Teams whose users connect their own apps to an AI.
why_it_matters: The user gets the part of the app one hub exposes, and every gap becomes new code in the product.
why_hard: Each hub has its own sign-in, scopes and tools, so combining them means mapping which hub serves which action, and that mapping is usually written by hand.
existing_attempts: One integration hub per product, and hand-written adapters for what it misses.

problem: A system often already has enduring integrations, such as its own AI tool registry, LLM platform and guardrails, and the AI cannot reach them or does not use them.
who_has_it: Teams that run AI inside an enterprise system.
why_it_matters: Duplicate tools and unguarded calls appear beside the ones the system already governs.
why_hard: Each system declares its integrations in its own way.
existing_attempts: Hand-wired connections per product.

problem: People often imply their priorities instead of stating them, so an AI weighs everything the same or guesses.
who_has_it: People who delegate to AI Representatives.
why_it_matters: Wrong weights spend effort on what matters less.
why_hard: The priorities are subtle, change over time and sit in how a person acts.
existing_attempts: Asking the person to rank everything.

problem: The questions, decisions and approvals an AI puts to a person reach them in the order they arrived, whatever each one unblocks, so the answer that would free five waiting tasks sits behind a question nothing waits on, and a person with many open asks is shown all of them at once.
who_has_it: People whose AI Representatives need answers from them.
why_it_matters: A person's attention is the scarcest input the system has: work stays blocked while a question that matters waits behind ones that do not, and a flood of asks teaches the person to stop answering.
why_hard: What an ask unblocks is spread over other items (the work waiting for it), its effort and deadline are only sometimes recorded, and how many asks a person welcomes at once differs by person.
existing_attempts: Putting asks in a queue by age and asking Judgment Calls only whether to ask.

problem: The milestones of the solutions of a person's intents (what each solution is to reach next, with its target time and what it depends on) are held as a flat list, so the AI cannot tell which matters most to the person: a milestone others depend on, one with a near target time and one the person said they care most about look alike, and the AI orders its own work and its questions without knowing.
who_has_it: People who delegate to AI Representatives and hold many goals at once.
why_it_matters: The AI spends its effort and its questions on whatever it was last shown, and the goal the person would pick first waits.
why_hard: The order is in what the person says, in how they react to what the AI does, in target times, in which milestone depends on which and in what reaching one unblocks, and none of it is one field, and a milestone may have no metric value to compare.
existing_attempts: Asking the person to rank every milestone, and listing them by when they were created.

problem: The work the AI is about to start unasked is started in the order it became due, so a daily chore can run before the report the person is waiting for.
who_has_it: People whose AI Representatives work without being asked.
why_it_matters: The first unasked work spends the budget and the person's trust, so starting the wrong thing first costs more than starting it late.
why_hard: Due work arrives from schedules, requests and events with no common measure of what matters, and the person's own wishes sit elsewhere.
existing_attempts: Running every due schedule in the order the clock made it due.

problem: Most requests are answered without a stated target, so it is hard to say whether the goal was met or whether a second try was better.
who_has_it: Anyone who asks an AI for a result.
why_it_matters: Without a target, the AI stops when its own answer looks finished to it.
why_hard: Requests state intent in words, and success depends on the person and the goal above it.
existing_attempts: A final check by the same model that did the work.

problem: A draft that does not meet the goal condition is sent as final after one pass, or hands the work back to the person, although means that could meet it were never tried.
who_has_it: Anyone who asks an AI for a result.
why_it_matters: The person must do work the AI could have done, or concludes it cannot, and asks again.
why_hard: Whether means remain, whether the remaining work is short enough to wait for, and whether a try is safe are different facts, and a write must never be repeated.
existing_attempts: A single regenerate pass with the same material, and a question to the person.

problem: Work that touches several solutions is judged in one broad pass from general knowledge, or a relevant solution, a scope above it or a solution relying on it is never considered at all.
who_has_it: Anyone whose AI acts on a system described by ESOI records.
why_it_matters: What a solution's own records hold (a measured loss, a milestone, a lesson) is missed, so the AI repeats a known mistake or breaks how parts combine.
why_hard: Which solutions a request concerns is a classification of its own, and giving each one its own pass costs more calls.
existing_attempts: One prompt with the whole records tree, or retrieval of records by similarity with no pass per solution.

problem: In many assistants each request starts mostly fresh: what happened before, what stays true and what the AI is working toward are kept only as far as the chat history or a few saved notes reach.
who_has_it: People who work with an AI over weeks and months.
why_it_matters: The person repeats themselves and the AI cannot carry a goal across requests.
why_hard: Memory, standing facts and objectives age differently and need different upkeep.
existing_attempts: Long chat histories, saved memories and manual notes.

problem: As standing instructions and corrections pile up, they are often all added to every task's prompt, so cost grows and quality can fall.
who_has_it: Anyone who runs an AI over many kinds of task.
why_it_matters: Prompt size is cost on every call, and unrelated instructions distract the model.
why_hard: The relevant instructions differ by task and are not labelled.
existing_attempts: One long system prompt.

problem: What the Mind sees for a request comes from two sources, the system's internal context and the outside, and each product wires both to the Mind its own way.
who_has_it: Teams that build an AI that plans and answers.
why_it_matters: A request is answered from one source only when the other is not wired.
why_hard: The two sources differ in cost, trust and speed, so weighing them against each other for one request is not simple.
existing_attempts: Separate prompts for retrieved context and for web results.
auto_status: open: unmeasured the-mind, the-assembler, the-subconscious, the-world, context-intake

problem: An AI that acts only when asked misses the standing work (a daily review, a weekly report) and the moment something changed, so people must remember to ask.
who_has_it: Anyone who wants the system to do standing work on time.
why_it_matters: Standing work that depends on a person remembering is done late or not at all.
why_hard: Simple schedules go wrong in quiet ways: one late run shifts every later one, an evening run is read in the wrong time zone, and an unreadable time can stop a schedule.
existing_attempts: Cron jobs, reminders, and the scheduled tasks some assistants offer, each set up by hand.

problem: Standing work for a person often falls on certain days of the week and a time of day in that person's own time zone (a review on weekday mornings, a report on Friday afternoons), and a late start is still worth doing for a while but not forever. A fixed interval or a calendar period cannot say that: 'every 24 hours' drifts off the time of day, and 'once a day' does not know weekends or whether the moment has come yet.
who_has_it: Anyone whose recurring work follows a working week in their own time zone.
why_it_matters: Work that starts at the wrong hour, on a rest day or a day late interrupts people or is missed, and a clock change shifts it by an hour without anyone noticing.
why_hard: The moment a time of day arrives depends on the time zone and its daylight-saving changes (a local time can happen twice or not at all), a window that opens near midnight reaches into the next day, and a run that is only slightly late should still count while one that is hours late should wait for the next occasion.
existing_attempts: Cron expressions and calendar reminders, each written by hand per zone and unaware of whether the last run already covered the occasion.

problem: Work that repeats unattended drifts into re-reading a number that cannot move, writing briefs and drafts that no one acts on, staging every item for approval and reporting the same missing access each run, so each run looks busy while little outside it changes.
who_has_it: Anyone who sets a system to do recurring work unattended and the people who write its standing instructions.
why_it_matters: Standing work exists to change something outside itself each time it runs; a run that only reports leaves the person with the same work and a growing pile of text.
why_hard: Each report looks like progress, a blocker repeated is easy to mistake for a status, and the instructions of a recurring run are written once and rarely rated against what the runs did.
existing_attempts: A schedule that starts the run on time (the triggers of this solution), approval of every item, and a summary at the end of each run.

problem: A task is shown too much of a codebase, the wrong part of it, or context it never needed, so the model pays for noise or misses the file that matters.
who_has_it: Any assistant that answers or edits against a repository or a folder of documents; Quest AI's context selection is the first consumer.
why_it_matters: Every token of irrelevant context costs money and attention, and a missing file makes the answer wrong or invented; a request that needs nothing from the corpus should not be sent any.
why_hard: Keywords find exact names but not the topic, meaning search finds the topic but not the exact name, and neither knows which files change together, which are close in the import graph or when to stay silent. Labels are costly and the best method differs by corpus.
existing_attempts: BM25 and vector search (the context-assembler arms), hybrid rank fusion, cross-encoder and model rerankers, repository maps such as Aider's, learned rerankers trained on a team's own history.

problem: An assembled system is mostly measured part by part, and whole-system checks are usually hand-run demos, so few teams have a repeatable, recorded way to see whether it behaves as one capable assistant: knowing what it may do, asking before anything irreversible and saying truthfully what it did.
who_has_it: People who use an AI built from many parts, and the teams that assemble it.
why_it_matters: Each part can pass its own test while the whole forgets a promise, acts without asking or reports work it did not do, and the user is the one who finds out.
why_hard: The user's seat spans every part, so no single part's metric sees the failure, and a fair score has to weigh capability together with consent and honesty, which need real tasks to test.
existing_attempts: Benchmarks of each part, end-to-end tests, and hand-run demos, usually with no recorded score for consent or honesty.

problem: One product's prompts and settings creep into shared code, so others have to find and strip them out before they can reuse it.
who_has_it: Teams building AI systems from open-source parts.
why_it_matters: Shared code that carries one product's wording or defaults behaves oddly for other products, and each case has to be found by hand.
why_hard: Product details enter a little at a time, through prompts, defaults and examples, and each looks harmless where it is added.
existing_attempts: Code review, and searching the code for the product's name.

problem: When each part that needs a model chooses and calls it its own way, tier choice, cost and failover are repeated in each part and drift apart.
who_has_it: Teams whose parts all call models.
why_it_matters: A price or vendor change then needs a change in every part.
why_hard: Models, prices and failures change weekly, and each part sees only its own calls.
existing_attempts: A model name written into each part.

problem: Each product wires its own integrations and finds a person's data its own way, so a new kind of integration means new code and a person's data locations are asked for again by every product.
who_has_it: Teams whose users want the AI to use tools and their own data.
why_it_matters: Users get the tools a team had time to wire, and the AI uses the first tool wired rather than the best.
why_hard: Tools and integrations in one category differ in coverage, cost and reliability, and change often.
existing_attempts: Hand-written integration code per product.

problem: A deep run, left unattended, writes or deletes outside the files its goal named, or reads a key or private file and carries it into a prompt, a reply or a file.
who_has_it: Anyone who hands a run to an agent they are not watching, and the person whose data the folder holds.
why_it_matters: A change nobody asked for or a leaked key cannot be taken back; it ends trust in unattended work.
why_hard: Shell access is what makes a run useful and also what makes it dangerous; the run runs with permission prompts skipped because nobody is there to answer them; a secret is only recognisable by what it is for.
existing_attempts: The hub loop runs commands in a bubblewrap sandbox with the disk read-only and refuses a floor of commands; Folder View leaves risky folders out and says so. The hub-framed native run is told to treat everything it reads as data and never to open a secret, takes a permission mode (the CLI's own: acceptEdits, auto, plan and the rest) and an optional bubblewrap sandbox (the folder, its scratch folder and the CLI's config writable, network on or off), and reports each file it wrote and each command it ran outside the working folder. Hub-initiated iteration never runs on what only a person can supply: Goal Completion's stop decision answers ask. Still open: the defaults are the CLI's skipped permissions and no sandbox (a person's own Claude Code session asks the person, and an unattended lane does not, so a consumer chooses the mode and the sandbox); nothing checks what the native session's tools read, so a secret read is not detected; the defence against an instruction hidden in a page or file is the frame's own sentence and the outside-the-folder report, with no content filter, so a page can still steer the session inside what its permissions allow.

problem: A run says the goal is met when a step failed, a figure is made up, a file it names does not exist, or only part of the work was done.
who_has_it: The person who acts on the report, and the consumer that marks a task done.
why_it_matters: A false done is acted on: it hides the failure until it costs more.
why_hard: A model writes its own report from what it believes it did; a check the model wrote can be as wrong as the work; only some claims (a figure, a file name) can be checked by code.
existing_attempts: The hub loop accepts a report only when its actions succeeded and a check passed, and the code check lists figures no source holds and files the folder lacks (used after a native session too); hidden tests in the hard cases. Goal Completion has an independent reviewer arm (independent_review): it reads the last outcome without the worker's claim or the verdict it was handed, and the hub's own iteration (resume, repeated nudge, rework of a part) is decided only on that reading, so a claim of success never ends or extends the iteration; it is selected by Goal Completion's metric (a few scripted misleading-claim and shallow-check cases). Still open: its second reading shares the code of the evidence standard, so a requirement the standard cannot see is invisible to both; it does not yet judge the truth of a consumer's final report, and a second model reading the work is not built or measured.

problem: A run repeats a failing command, circles between two steps or keeps calling the model until the budget or the wall clock ends it.
who_has_it: Whoever pays for the subscription or the key, and the lane that is held by a run that never ends.
why_it_matters: Cost and a blocked lane, with no result.
why_hard: A repeated step looks like progress to the model; a spend ceiling set too low cuts off real work; the two loops (hub and CLI) count limits differently.
existing_attempts: The hub loop has a call limit and refuses a command that failed twice with the same error; the stream runner has a wall clock and a liveness review. Every harness that holds a session (the stream runner, the native run and the hub's text loop) has a default ceiling on spend and on time (20 dollars and 4 hours, high enough that ordinary work never meets it), with UNLIMITED only when a caller says so; at 80 percent of either the session is steered once to a safe stopping point (finish the step in hand, leave things consistent, report what is done, what is left and how to resume), and at the limit it is stopped like a person's stop with the work kept and resumable (the native run also passes the remaining dollars to the CLI as a backstop). Only the hub's own iteration is judged: Goal Completion's stop decision ends a plateau, an oscillation, a regress and a step whose cost exceeds its expected gain, obeys what the person stated, and bounds unasked iteration at five. A person's own session runs until a ceiling they can raise, as in Claude Code. Still open: spend is the CLI's figure at the end of a session and an estimate from the session record while it runs; a text loop's saved session does not carry its spend, so a resume starts a fresh window; a helper's nudges inside the text loop are bounded by the shared call counter, not the decision; the one-shot, Codex, opencode and ACP arms have no ceiling of their own; the ceilings and the stop thresholds are set from measured hard cases and scripted histories, not from real runs.

problem: A web page, a file or a command output holds text that tells the agent to do something, and the run does it.
who_has_it: Any run that reads the web or a person's files.
why_it_matters: The run acts with the person's authority on a stranger's words.
why_hard: To a model, instructions and data are both text; the more tools a run has, the more a planted line can do.
existing_attempts: The hub frame tells the run to treat what it reads as data. What a planted line can do is bounded by structure, not by the prompt: the native run's permission mode and optional sandbox (what may be written and run), its report of everything written or run outside the folder, and the ceilings on money and time. What the person stated about iteration (keep going, one pass) reaches the hub's stop decision only as an input a consumer resolved from the Representative, Guidance and the request, never from text a run read, so a planted line cannot extend or end hub-initiated iteration. Still open: the instruction-versus-data rule itself is a prompt, nothing detects an injected instruction in content, the defaults leave the sandbox off, and no metric measures it yet.

problem: A run raises a question or a decision for a fact it could have found itself, for example a date in a file's history, a rate in a database table or a figure on the web.
who_has_it: The person who is not there to answer, and the consumer that marks the task as needing them.
why_it_matters: Work stops at the first missing fact; the person is interrupted for what a competent colleague would have looked up.
why_hard: A fact hidden behind a non-obvious route looks missing; a run that is too eager invents a value instead; the right balance depends on the tools the run has.
existing_attempts: A discover-before-asking rule in the hub frame and a tool surface that reaches files, history, a database file, command output and the web (measured free for each arm); the two long hard cases test it, with a hidden test for the real value. Pending: no standing metric stage for it in the solution record.

problem: A command an agent runs never ends, prints more than the prompt can hold, is refused for a harmless reason, or leaves files in a temporary folder that the next command no longer sees.
who_has_it: Any harness that executes the commands a model writes.
why_it_matters: A hung command holds the run, a flood spends the budget, and a lost file makes a long run redo or fail its earlier steps (a real lane run lost its scripts between commands).
why_hard: A command can start children that outlive it; output size is not known in advance; confinement that works by reading words misses programs that open paths themselves; a private temporary folder per command is the safe default and the wrong one for a multi-step job.
existing_attempts: A process group killed at a timeout, clipped output, a refusal floor, a bubblewrap sandbox with a scratch folder bound for the whole session.

problem: A harness asks a model for its actions in a private text protocol, so the model spends calls on the protocol, sometimes writes its trained markup instead (which the parser ignores) and behaves less resourcefully than in its provider's own tool loop.
who_has_it: Teams that build their own harness and the people who rely on its runs.
why_it_matters: Four real runs of a long task failed in part on this, and the same task was finished by the provider's own agent.
why_hard: A model can be taught a format in a prompt and appear to follow it; the failure shows only on long tool-heavy work; each provider trains and recommends a different format.
existing_attempts: Provider agents with their trained tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI), Aider's edit format per model, a lenient parser for the markup a model writes by habit.

problem: A web or mobile frontend that is not the terminal cannot show a session: the harness events and controls are Python objects, and each consumer's backend invents its own wire, so each screen drops cost, helpers, changed files, the acknowledgement of a steer or the pending question, or carries terminal wording it cannot draw.
who_has_it: Teams who put an AI's work on a page or in an app, and the people who watch it there.
why_it_matters: A person on a page has the same need to see, stop and steer as one in a terminal; a frontend that loses the steer acknowledgement or the open question makes them act blind.
why_hard: The data must be complete and plain at once, carry nothing that only makes sense in a terminal, survive a reconnect, and tolerate event kinds a newer harness adds.
existing_attempts: Each consumer's own backend maps its stream to its own page; protocols such as the Agent Client Protocol carry a session between an agent and an editor but not the run facts a page draws.

problem: When sub-agents work on specific solutions, the person cannot tell which solutions are being worked on, which sub-agent is on which, what each does, or what a solution is for and how it connects, so the structure that guides the work is invisible while it runs.
who_has_it: People who delegate deep work that follows a hierarchy of solutions and want to see and check it.
why_it_matters: A person who cannot see the structure cannot tell whether the work follows the intent, and a flat list of agents hides the hierarchy that explains why each does what it does.
why_hard: The overview must stay small yet reach into each solution's fields and connections on request, for any interface, and an agent may name a solution the records do not hold.
existing_attempts: Agent trees in terminals list helpers and tasks without the solutions they serve; documentation sites show the records but not what is being worked on now.

problem: The hub can be run from a command line one input at a time, and each run starts without the earlier ones, so a person cannot try it or steer it by talking with it, answer a question it asks, or see what it is doing between one line and the next.
who_has_it: People trying the hub or working with it from a terminal.
why_it_matters: A person who cannot converse with the hub tries fewer inputs, answers its questions late or not at all, and judges it on one reply.
why_hard: A conversation needs the work, the questions and the commands drawn as they happen, and the same front door a script uses, so the session cannot reach into the hub's parts.
existing_attempts: A one-shot command per input, and scripts that call the front door in a loop; neither draws the work or a question for a person to answer.

problem: A cheap model asked for a decision in one prompt that mixes every kind of evidence (rules, past examples, descriptions, tool records) often picks wrongly, and the pick is seldom checked against the evidence it should rest on.
who_has_it: Anyone who runs an AI on a cheap model tier to place work, pick an option or reply to a person.
why_it_matters: A wrong pick or an unsupported claim reaches a person silently, and the cost of a stronger model on every decision is not affordable.
why_hard: A model that judges its own mixed prompt tends to repeat its first answer; one extra verify call over the same mixed evidence has not helped.
existing_attempts: One stronger model for every call; a single verify step after the pick.

problem: A check makes the same kind of mistake again and again, though each one was found (an eval failure, a person's correction, a disagreement that was settled), because the lesson stays in a log and does not reach the prompt.
who_has_it: Anyone whose AI is corrected by people or by its own evaluation and still repeats the error.
why_it_matters: People correct the same thing repeatedly and lose trust; evaluation failures are fixed one by one in code or prompt text with no record of what paid.
why_hard: Which lesson helps which check is not obvious, a lesson can overfit the cases it came from, and a line that helped once can stop helping.
existing_attempts: Editing prompts by hand after a failure; a pile of rules added to every prompt.

problem: Response quality is usually judged by one fixed standard, though what counts as high quality depends on the person, the situation and the goals above the request.
who_has_it: People whose AI answers well by a standard that is not theirs.
why_it_matters: A response can pass every check and still miss what this person needed.
why_hard: Preferences are partly implied, change with feedback and differ by context.
existing_attempts: A fixed rubric or a single judge prompt.

problem: A worker given one piece of a request is often not told the authority it carries or what done means for that piece.
who_has_it: People who delegate to an AI that delegates further.
why_it_matters: A worker may do too much, too little or the wrong thing, and it is hard to tell afterwards which.
why_hard: Authority and done-standards are rarely written down for sub-goals.
existing_attempts: A prompt that restates the request.

problem: A phrase that refers to a person, a goal or a post is matched to a candidate by the words they share, in several parts that each do it their own way, and none of them can say that no candidate is meant.
who_has_it: Anyone who runs an AI that writes to a shared tool of a team: owners, goals, posts.
why_it_matters: A wrong match overwrites what a person wrote (five people's goals were overwritten once) or pairs a post with an unrelated goal; the damage is silent and lands on someone else.
why_hard: Right matches and look-alikes share the same words, and a model that must always choose will choose.
existing_attempts: Substring and shared-word matching; a guard that limits which goals may be written, which contains the harm but does not fix the match.

problem: What a request asks of the system (to be told something, something done, text written, or not yet understood) is decided by several parts that each read the request their own way: an analyser, the plan itself, a cue check, a draft flag and guards after the plan.
who_has_it: Anyone who runs an AI that answers questions, does work and writes text from one chat.
why_it_matters: When the parts disagree a status question starts a long run, a count is answered without reading anything, and a cue naming a tracked milestone is described instead of acted on.
why_hard: The same words can ask for different things, and each part sees a different slice of the request and its context.
existing_attempts: A flag per failure, added where the failure was seen; guards that overturn the plan after it is made.

problem: New work piles onto a structure that has an experiment past its reevaluation, a solution with several implementations and no metric, a duplicate, a missed reuse or a milestone past its date, and nobody looks at the structure itself until the cost shows.
who_has_it: Anyone whose work is built on ESOI records.
why_it_matters: Structure is the most stable part so a flaw there is paid for by every later piece of work.
why_hard: Looking at the whole structure for every piece of work is costly, and a check that is wrong too often is ignored.
existing_attempts: The records' own checks (esoi check), a person's review, and run-step risk watching, which sees one step and not the structure.

problem: A piece of work in a local folder has files but no cards for them and no view of which files matter, so it reads too much, reads what is risky, or misses what it needs.
who_has_it: Any assistant that works in a folder of files on a person's computer or server.
why_it_matters: Every wrong file costs tokens at every call and buries the right one; a secret read into a prompt cannot be taken back.
why_hard: Folders differ by ecosystem and by person; grouping and choosing are different jobs that fail differently and need different measures.
existing_attempts: Cards written by hand or by a model, one card per file, repository maps, fixed lists of skipped names.

problem: How old each area's research is has to be worked out by hand, so stale recommendations go unnoticed.
who_has_it: Anyone who relies on the hub's recommendations.
why_it_matters: A recommendation can be months out of date and still be followed.
why_hard: The dates sit in many rows and each area has its own bar.
existing_attempts: Reading the registry by eye.

problem: Most products wire each connected system's operations by hand.
who_has_it: Teams that connect an AI to the systems they already use.
why_it_matters: Each connection is code to write, secure and keep current.
why_hard: Systems expose operations in different ways.
existing_attempts: A hand-written client per system, and MCP servers, which cover some systems but leave each product to choose and call the operations.

problem: A change to one file is routed to an agent session that costs and takes far more than the edit needs, or is hand-written for each product.
who_has_it: Anyone whose AI changes files.
why_it_matters: Cost and time per edit grow with the harness, not with the edit.
why_hard: A cheap one-call edit and an agent session can do different things, and telling which one a change needs is itself a judgment.
existing_attempts: Sending every change to an agent harness, or writing edit code for each product.

problem: A consumer whose knowledge lives in files has no cards for it until something writes them, and cards written once go stale as the files change.
who_has_it: Any team that points an AI at a repository or a folder of documents; Quest AI's lanes are the first consumer.
why_it_matters: Recall can only return what the store holds: a store that is empty, bloated or stale sends the AI to read whole folders or to act on old facts.
why_hard: Good grouping needs to know what belongs together. A model can judge that but costs money on every build; structure-only tools are free but group by calls and imports, which may not match how people ask.
existing_attempts: Quest AI's model-written topic cards; one card per source file in its evaluation; code graphs such as Graphify; repository maps such as Aider's.

problem: A piece of work in a folder of thousands of files is shown files from dependency, build and cache folders or notes that share a word with the goal, and can be shown files that hold credentials, backups or other people's private data, while the file it needs is missed.
who_has_it: Any harness that maps a working folder before its first model call, in any programming language; the hub's own work harness is the first consumer.
why_it_matters: Every wrong file costs tokens at every call and buries the right one; a secret read into a prompt cannot be taken back.
why_hard: Dependency and build folders have different names and markers in each ecosystem and the same names hold work elsewhere; shared words pick noise in a large folder; a risky folder can have an ordinary name.
existing_attempts: Fixed lists of skipped names, version-control ignore files, repository maps such as Aider's, retrieval over an index of the corpus.
